introduction.p: The Intermediate Value Theorem requires continuity on an interval. The Extreme Value Theorem requires continuity on a closed, bounded interval. The examples below show how their conclusions can fail when these conditions are removed. We will also distinguish a function value from its nearby limit.

subsection.p: Changing the value at x=0 cannot repair the two-sided limit. The problem is not the point itself. The problem is that the nearby values on the two sides head toward different numbers.

p.me: \text{A two-sided limit is about agreement from both sides.}

exercise.title: Why can changing the value at a jump never repair a two-sided limit?

statement.p: At a jump, the left-hand and right-hand limits disagree. In your own words, why is the problem not the point itself, and why does a two-sided limit demand agreement from both sides?

hint.p: Nearby values on the two sides are already heading toward different numbers. Relabeling the single center point cannot make those two neighborhoods share a target.

subsection.p: A removable discontinuity can be repaired by filling in one value. Infinite divergent behavior cannot. No choice of f(0) can keep the nearby values close to a finite number.

p.me: \infty\text{ describes unbounded behavior. It is not a real-number target.}

exercise.title: Why is \infty not a real-number target?

statement.p: The values of \frac1{x^2} grow beyond every fixed positive bound as x\to0. In your own words, why is that infinite behavior not a finite limit, and why can no choice of a value at the missing point keep the nearby outputs close to a real number L?

hint.p: A finite limit requires outputs to settle inside some \varepsilon-window around a real target. Unbounded growth refuses every such window. Filling one point cannot cage an exploding neighborhood.

p.me: \text{The Intermediate Value Theorem is a no-jump theorem.}

exercise.title: Which hypothesis of the Intermediate Value Theorem must be checked?

statement.p: The Intermediate Value Theorem is a no-jump theorem: continuous graph plus endpoint values imply that intermediate heights are hit. In your own words, why does dropping continuity let a function skip a height, and what should you check before using the theorem to prove that an equation has a solution?

hint.p: A theorem is a machine with conditions. If the graph can jump, an intermediate value is no longer guaranteed. Check continuity on the closed interval first.

subsection.title: The Extreme Value Theorem fails on an open interval
subsection.p: The Extreme Value Theorem said:

p.em: continuous on [a,b] \Longrightarrow absolute maximum and minimum are reached.

subsection.p: The closed interval [a,b] includes its endpoints. If the endpoints are missing, the conclusion can fail.
Consider
on the open interval
The function is continuous at every point of its domain. Its values get close to 1, but never equal 1, because x=1 is not in the interval.
So f has no absolute maximum on (0,1).
The values also get close to 0, but never equal 0, because x=0 is not in the interval.
So f has no absolute minimum on (0,1).

figure.caption: On (0,1), the function f(x)=x approaches its lowest and highest possible values but never reaches them.

description.p: On (0,1), the function f(x)=x approaches its lowest and highest possible values but never reaches them.

subsection.p: The problem is not the formula. The formula f(x)=x is perfectly continuous. The problem is the domain. The endpoints are missing.

p.me: \text{For the Extreme Value Theorem, endpoints matter.}

exercise.title: Which Extreme Value Theorem hypotheses fail in these examples?

statement.p: On an open interval, f(x)=x approaches its apparent highest and lowest values without reaching them. On [0,\infty), the same formula has no largest value. In your own words, why do both closed and bounded matter, and what does it mean to say that a theorem’s output is no longer guaranteed when a condition is missing?

hint.p: Endpoints can be the place where a max or min is attained. An interval that stretches forever can let values escape. The examples are reminders of what the theorem actually says, not exceptions to it.
